Based on the Fed’s “Household Debt – Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA) Debt‑to‑Income Ratio” table (which lists the quarterly ranges for each MSA), the New Jersey‑based MSAs that reached or exceeded a 1.35 ratio in Q 1 2023 are:

| MSA (New Jersey‑based) | Debt‑to‑Income Ratio range for Q 1 2023 |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Allentown‑Bethlehem‑Easton, PA‑NJ | 1.25 – 1.35 |
| Atlantic City‑Hammonton, NJ | 1.79 – 2.06 |
| Vineland, NJ | 1.25 – 1.35 |

*Sources:* The Fed table shows the Q 1 2023 range for each MSA (e.g., “Allentown‑Bethlehem‑Easton, PA‑NJ MSA 1.25 1.35”, “Atlantic City‑Hammonton, NJ MSA 1.79 2.06”, and “Vineland, NJ MSA 1.25 1.35”). These are the only New Jersey‑located MSAs whose upper limits reach 1.35 or higher in Q 1 2023.

It might refer to a "HofD" dataset from County-level (MSA). There is a dataset "Household Debt and Credit: Monthly" including MSA/COMSTAT? The "Federal Reserve's County Credit and Mortgage" dataset?

Household Debt Balances Decrease Slightly in June
The latest _Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit_ shows total U.S. household debt decreasing by $13 billion, or 0.1 percent, to reach $18.8 trillion in the second quarter of 2026. Aggregate delinquency rates improved slightly, with 4.7 percent of outstanding debt in some stage of delinquency. Mortgage balances declined to $13.1 trillion and home equity lines of credit balances rose to $459 billion at the end of June.
Background
The large increases in consumer debt and defaults—of mortgage debt in particular—during the Great Recession highlighted the importance of understanding the liabilities reflected on household balance sheets. To that end, one of the CMD’s large data collection projects is the New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel, which is constructed from a nationally representative random sample of Equifax credit report data. Analysis of this dataset is regularly reported in the CMD’s Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit. The dataset can be used to calculate national and regional aggregate measures of individual- and household-level credit balances, and delinquencies by product type. The Consumer Credit Panel also provides new insights into the extent and nature of heterogeneity of debt and delinquencies across individuals and households.

Household Debt Balances Decrease Slightly in June
The latest _Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit_ shows total U.S. household debt decreasing by $13 billion, or 0.1 percent, to reach $18.8 trillion in the second quarter of 2026. Aggregate delinquency rates improved slightly, with 4.7 percent of outstanding debt in some stage of delinquency. Mortgage balances declined to $13.1 trillion and home equity lines of credit balances rose to $459 billion at the end of June.
Background
The large increases in consumer debt and defaults—of mortgage debt in particular—during the Great Recession highlighted the importance of understanding the liabilities reflected on household balance sheets. To that end, one of the CMD’s large data collection projects is the New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel, which is constructed from a nationally representative random sample of Equifax credit report data. Analysis of this dataset is regularly reported in the CMD’s Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit. The dataset can be used to calculate national and regional aggregate measures of individual- and household-level credit balances, and delinquencies by product type. The Consumer Credit Panel also provides new insights into the extent and nature of heterogeneity of debt and delinquencies across individuals and households.

Household Debt Balances Decrease Slightly in June
The latest _Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit_ shows total U.S. household debt decreasing by $13 billion, or 0.1 percent, to reach $18.8 trillion in the second quarter of 2026. Aggregate delinquency rates improved slightly, with 4.7 percent of outstanding debt in some stage of delinquency. Mortgage balances declined to $13.1 trillion and home equity lines of credit balances rose to $459 billion at the end of June.
Background
The large increases in consumer debt and defaults—of mortgage debt in particular—during the Great Recession highlighted the importance of understanding the liabilities reflected on household balance sheets. To that end, one of the CMD’s large data collection projects is the New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel, which is constructed from a nationally representative random sample of Equifax credit report data. Analysis of this dataset is regularly reported in the CMD’s Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit. The dataset can be used to calculate national and regional aggregate measures of individual- and household-level credit balances, and delinquencies by product type. The Consumer Credit Panel also provides new insights into the extent and nature of heterogeneity of debt and delinquencies across individuals and households.
